questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the core statistical intuition behind the Flicker Metric?
options: Stability is the inverse of variance
Stability is the inverse of mean
Flicker is the sum of pixel values
Stability is the product of time and space
questions.answer: Stability is the inverse of variance
questions.why: The lesson states: 'Our intuition is simple: Stability is the inverse of variance.' It explains that if pixel values do not change over time, their variance is zero, indicating perfect stability.

questions.q: In the provided mathematical definition, what does the symbol $\bar{v}_{c,h,w}$ represent?
options: The variance of the pixel at location (c, h, w)
The mean value of that pixel over time
The total number of frames in the video
The spatial width of the video tensor
questions.answer: The mean value of that pixel over time
questions.why: The lesson explicitly defines $\bar{v}_{c,h,w}$ as 'the mean value of that pixel over time' in the formula for temporal variance.

questions.q: Why is it a common mistake to apply the raw Flicker Metric to a video of a fast-moving car without prior processing?
options: Because the car's color changes randomly
Because the metric would measure motion as flicker
Because the video has too few frames
Because the car is not in the center of the frame
questions.answer: Because the metric would measure motion as flicker
questions.why: The 'Common mistakes' section states: 'If you apply this metric to a video of a fast-moving car, you will get a high score. This is not flicker; it is motion.' It advises using optical flow to align frames first.

questions.q: In PyTorch, if a video tensor has the shape $(T, C, H, W)$, along which dimension index must you compute the variance to correctly measure temporal flicker?
questions.why: The lesson states: 'In PyTorch, if your tensor is shaped $(T, C, H, W)$, you must compute variance along `dim=0`.' It warns that using dim=1 would measure color inconsistency instead.
